mcqs.question: How does an 'undecidable' problem differ from an 'NP-hard' problem?
options: NP-hard problems are solvable but believed to require exponential time; undecidable problems have no algorithm at all, for any amount of time
They're the same thing, just different names used by different textbooks
Undecidable problems are a subset of NP-hard problems
NP-hard means 'impossible to solve'; undecidable means 'slow to solve'
mcqs.explanation: NP-hard problems (like TSP) are decidable — an algorithm exists and will eventually give the correct answer, it just may take exponential time in the worst case. Undecidable problems (like the halting problem) have no correct algorithm whatsoever, regardless of how much time is allowed. These are different axes entirely (solvability vs. efficiency), not variations of the same idea.

mcqs.question: In the diagonalization proof of the halting problem, why does constructing D(P) — which does the opposite of what H predicts — prove that H can't exist?
options: Because D(D) is undefined and therefore the proof doesn't actually work
Because asking whether D(D) halts leads to a contradiction no matter what H(D,D) answers, so no correct H can exist
Because D always halts, which contradicts the definition of a Turing machine
Because H can simply refuse to answer for D, avoiding the contradiction
mcqs.explanation: The construction forces a contradiction in both cases: if H predicts D(D) halts, D is built to loop instead; if H predicts D(D) loops, D is built to halt instead. Since H must give one of these two answers and both lead to H being wrong, no consistently correct H can exist. A halting-checker is assumed total (must answer for every input), so 'refusing to answer' isn't an option available to H by the problem's own definition.
